task.goal: Teach beginning musicians to hear and correct uneven rhythm in a group rehearsal.
hard_constraints: One instructor, eight beginners, three 30-minute sessions, and no recording app.
Do not single out a learner publicly or require extra home equipment.
Separate tempo drift from missed beats and check improvement on an unfamiliar pattern.
task.available_resources: Clapping, metronome already owned by instructor, paper marks.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Predict the pulse through silent gaps
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Main mechanism: learners maintain an internal pulse while the metronome briefly disappears, then use its return to hear tempo drift. Counting positions separately helps distinguish drift from missed beats. This could work by making two different errors audible: the whole pulse moving versus an expected clap being absent.

Use one instructor, eight learners clapping together, the existing metronome, and paper showing eight numbered beat positions. Explain that everyone is testing a group skill; give only group feedback and never request individual demonstrations. Assume learners can hear the metronome and understand a steady spoken count. Start slowly enough for comfortable participation.

Session 1, 30 minutes: spend five minutes establishing pulse; five hearing instructor demonstrations of acceleration versus an omitted clap; fifteen alternating eight-beat group clapping with metronome-supported counting; and five discussing what changed. An omitted clap leaves its numbered position intact: continue counting rather than restarting.

Session 2: spend five minutes reviewing, fifteen alternating audible clicks with short silent intervals while learners continue clapping, five diagnosing examples, and five reflecting. The instructor mutes and restores the running metronome if possible. Otherwise, learners stop clapping for selected beats while clicks continue; this simpler version provides less evidence about independent pulse maintenance. Diagnose drift from repeated claps progressively separating from clicks; diagnose omissions from empty expected positions followed by correctly placed claps.

Session 3: spend ten minutes on longer gaps, ten alternating full clapping and paper-marked rests, and ten on the unfamiliar-pattern check below. Correction cues are specific: ‘keep the spacing’ for drift and ‘keep counting through the empty position’ for omissions. Group sound can conceal individual difficulties, so this supports group improvement without establishing individual mastery.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: At the start and end of session 3, compare two previously unused eight-beat patterns with equal numbers of claps and rests. Randomly choose their order. For each, hear one supported attempt and one short silent-gap attempt. On paper, tally group omissions separately from progressive displacement against returning clicks; mark unclear cases as uncertain. Compare with ordinary continuous-click practice of equal duration. If silent-gap practice produces no clearer return alignment, or increases omissions, its proposed benefit is unsupported at this difficulty. One group and two patterns provide only a small practical check.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Build rhythm around a shared pulse role
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Main mechanism: separate keeping time from producing the rhythm, then rotate those responsibilities. A steady subgroup provides an audible reference against which the other subgroup can hear whether its rhythm accelerates, slows, or loses an event. Reducing simultaneous demands may help beginners correct one problem at a time.

Use the instructor’s metronome, clapping, and paper strips with eight numbered positions. Four learners clap every beat softly; four clap only marked positions. Switch roles frequently, assign roles by seating rather than ability, and describe both as equally necessary. Nobody performs alone. This assumes the two sound layers remain distinguishable; the pulse group can clap softly while the pattern group claps at ordinary volume. If the room is too loud, shorten turns and lower both groups’ volume.

Session 1, 30 minutes: five minutes establish a shared pulse, five hear instructor examples of drift and omission, fifteen practise the two roles with frequent switches, and five review. Keep the metronome audible. Teach that an omitted clap does not remove a beat: rejoin at the next numbered position. Drift means successive claps move increasingly ahead of or behind the reference.

Session 2: five minutes review, twenty alternate short supported and unsupported rounds, and five reflect. Before each unsupported round, establish the pulse with the metronome; restore clicks afterward to check whether the pulse subgroup itself drifted. If it did, reset together rather than treating its timing as authoritative. For omissions, simplify the marked pattern while retaining eight positions; for drift, return briefly to all-beat clapping.

Session 3: ten minutes rotate roles on familiar patterns, ten bring everyone together on the same pattern, and ten test unfamiliar patterns. The intended outcome is transferring the reference-pulse habit into full-group playing. Its main limit is dependence on the pulse subgroup: success during divided roles may disappear when everyone must manage both timing and pattern.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Use two unfamiliar patterns matched for length, clap count, and rests. Practise one for three minutes with divided roles and the other for three minutes with everyone clapping together, using equal metronome support. Then perform each with everyone together, checking against clicks. The instructor tallies omitted events and progressive timing displacement separately, without naming learners. Choose pattern assignment by a simple draw. If the divided-role pattern performs no better once the pulse subgroup is removed, the transfer mechanism is unsupported. Pattern differences and collective masking limit conclusions.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Hear the error, choose the repair
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Main mechanism: teach an explicit listening decision before asking for correction. Beginners practise distinguishing ‘the spaces changed’ from ‘an event disappeared,’ then select the matching repair. This may prevent a missed clap from causing a restart or rush, and prevent tempo drift from being treated merely as a counting mistake.

The instructor uses clapping demonstrations, the existing metronome, and paper marked ‘spacing,’ ‘missing,’ and ‘unclear.’ Learners point privately to a mark held close to themselves; the instructor reports only group trends. All performance remains collective. Assume the instructor can demonstrate the two errors clearly enough at a slow tempo. Mixed or ambiguous errors are labelled unclear rather than forced into a category.

Session 1, 30 minutes: five minutes establish eight steady beats; ten compare instructor demonstrations against audible clicks; ten alternate listening decisions with group imitation of a correct version; five review. Demonstrate drift by progressively shortening or lengthening intervals while preserving all expected events. Demonstrate an omission by leaving one clap out while keeping subsequent claps on their original beats. Include correct examples so learners do not assume every demonstration is wrong.

Session 2: five minutes review, ten diagnose fresh examples, ten practise the corresponding repairs, and five reflect. For spacing errors, return to steady all-beat clapping with clicks before restoring the pattern. For omissions, speak all eight beat numbers and clap only paper-marked events, preserving silent positions. Alternate repairs and gradually remove the instructor’s verbal cue so learners choose from what they hear.

Session 3: five minutes review, ten use a listen–choose–retry cycle during group clapping, and fifteen complete the unfamiliar-pattern check. The instructor may identify the group error when it is audible, but should not attribute it to a learner. This approach primarily builds recognition and repair selection; accurate labels alone do not establish improved timing, and dense group sound may conceal omissions.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Before instruction and during session 3, present different short sets containing steady examples, drift, and omissions; tally anonymous choices to check listening discrimination. Then compare two unfamiliar, equally sparse eight-beat patterns. Give one a brief diagnosis-and-selected-repair cycle and the other equal-duration repetition with ‘try again’ feedback. Assess the next group attempt against the metronome, tallying omissions separately from drift. If identification improves but performance does not, the method has taught recognition without demonstrated correction. If selected repairs do no better than repetition, their added value remains unproven.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Fill the spaces, then fade the subdivision
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Main mechanism: insert quiet spoken halfway counts between beats, then gradually remove them. These intermediate time points may help beginners keep equal spacing across rests and avoid rushing toward the next clap. Paper separates expected claps from deliberate rests. The proposed benefit comes from subdividing long intervals into smaller, repeatable intervals.

Use only collective clapping, the instructor’s metronome, and paper strips showing eight numbered beats with clap marks. Everyone participates together; nobody demonstrates alone or receives named feedback. Assume learners can comfortably say ‘one-and, two-and’ at a slow tempo and hear the clicks beneath quiet speech. Subdivision can initially increase cognitive load, so introduce it on all-beat clapping before adding rests.

Session 1, 30 minutes: spend five minutes matching claps to clicks; five hearing instructor examples of tempo drift and missed claps; ten speaking numbers on clicks and ‘and’ halfway between them; and ten clapping marked beats while maintaining quiet subdivision. Explain that drift means successive claps move progressively ahead of or behind clicks. A missed clap leaves an expected position empty while later claps retain their timing. Deliberate paper-marked rests are neither error.

Session 2: five minutes review, fifteen alternate four repetitions with spoken subdivision and four with numbers alone, five practise recovery, and five reflect. For drift, restore even halfway counts. For a missed clap, continue counting and rejoin at the next marked position. Give only group feedback; call mixed or inaudible errors uncertain.

Session 3: ten minutes fade from spoken subdivision to silent counting, five rehearse familiar patterns without speech, and fifteen conduct the transfer check. This may support spacing, but dependence on speech or difficulty coordinating speech and claps could prevent transfer. Group sound also masks individual omissions.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: In session 3, introduce two unfamiliar eight-beat patterns matched for clap count and longest rest. Give each one metronome-supported baseline attempt. Draw lots to assign two minutes of subdivision practice to one and two minutes of ordinary numbered-count practice to the other. Then perform both without speech, with clicks audible. On paper, compare baseline-to-final changes in progressive displacement and clearly audible missing expected group claps separately; mark ambiguous cases uncertain. If subdivision yields no greater improvement, or adds omissions, its added value is unsupported in this rehearsal. Two patterns and collective observation provide only a preliminary check.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Keep the motion through the rests
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Main mechanism: make clapping part of a continuous, comfortable hand movement. Hands approach on each beat and separate between beats; on a marked rest, make the same approach without contact. This gives silent positions a physical action, potentially preventing learners from shortening rests or losing their place. Gradually reduce the movement so the group can transfer the timing to ordinary clapping. The proposed mechanism is continuity of movement across silence.

Use the instructor’s metronome and paper showing eight numbered positions, with circles for claps and dashes for rests. Assume learners can comfortably make repeated small hand movements and hear the clicks. Allow a smaller movement where needed. All eight practise together; feedback concerns the group, with no solo demonstrations or named corrections.

Session 1, 30 minutes: five minutes establish comfortable claps against clicks; five hear the instructor demonstrate tempo drift versus an omitted clap; ten establish the repeating approach-and-release motion; ten alternate claps and silent approaches using the paper. Explain that drift progressively moves attacks ahead of or behind clicks. A missed clap leaves an expected circle silent, while subsequent attacks may remain correctly timed. Printed rests are intentional.

Session 2: five minutes review; fifteen alternate ordinary clapping with continuous-motion rounds; five practise recovering after an omission without restarting; five reflect. For drift, restore a small, even movement against clicks. For omissions, follow the numbered positions and join the next circle. Keep movements relaxed rather than imposing a precise gesture shape.

Session 3: ten minutes progressively shrink the motion; five practise familiar patterns with ordinary clapping; fifteen check unfamiliar patterns. This could fail if coordinating silent approaches adds difficulty or if timing depends on conspicuous movement. Collective sound can conceal individual omissions, so conclusions concern audible group performance.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Reserve two unfamiliar eight-beat patterns matched for clap count and rest length. During session 3, give each one ordinary-clapping baseline attempt with clicks. Draw lots: practise one for two minutes using continuous motion and the other for two minutes using ordinary clapping, with identical metronome support. Retest both using ordinary clapping. Tally clearly absent expected group attacks separately from progressive displacement against clicks; mark ambiguous cases uncertain. If motion practice produces no greater baseline-to-retest improvement, or increases omissions, its added value is unsupported here. This small comparison cannot establish individual improvement or rule out pattern differences.

EXPAND.title: Prepare the next clap before its beat
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: make hand preparation continuous and repeatable, reducing late claps caused by starting the movement only when the beat arrives. Learners open their hands smoothly between contacts and arrive at the next contact with the click. They then hear whether contacts remain evenly spaced. This targets movement execution rather than the prior routes’ internal-pulse prediction or error classification.

The instructor needs the owned metronome and paper with eight numbered positions. Assume learners can clap comfortably and hear quiet clicks. Offer small, comfortable movements; do not prescribe identical movement sizes. All eight work together, with no individual demonstrations or public scores.

Session 1, 30 minutes: five establish comfortable clapping; five watch the instructor contrast last-second preparation with smooth preparation; fifteen alternate ordinary clapping and continuous preparation against clicks; five discuss which contacts sounded early or late. Keep the tempo slow enough that preparation feels unhurried.

Session 2: five review, ten maintain the movement through paper-marked rests without making contact, ten alternate patterns with all-beat clapping, and five review. Progressive movement away from clicks indicates drift; an absent marked contact followed by correctly timed contacts indicates an omission. Correct drift by restoring comfortable movement spacing. For omissions, retain the movement through the empty position and rejoin at the next marked contact.

Session 3: five warm up, ten practise increasingly sparse patterns, ten check unfamiliar patterns, and five reflect. If movements create tension or distract from listening, reduce their size or return to ordinary clapping. Group feedback remains descriptive: ‘our contacts moved ahead’ or ‘one expected position sounded empty.’ Collective sound cannot establish individual mastery.
EXPAND.experiment: The instructor owns the trial. Reserve two equally sparse unfamiliar patterns for session 3. Give one three minutes of movement preparation and the other three minutes of the prior listen–choose–repair routine, assigning methods by a paper draw. Assess both with audible clicks and ordinary clapping, without movement reminders. Tally progressive displacement, clearly empty expected positions, and uncertain cases separately. Ask for private paper marks about effort or discomfort. Stop the movement exercise if discomfort occurs or omissions repeatedly increase. Retain it only if timing improves without greater effort or missed events; otherwise its additional motor demands have not earned their place.

EXPAND.title: Put a quiet halfway point inside each beat
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: use subdivision to shorten the interval learners must estimate. Quietly saying ‘one-and, two-and’ supplies a halfway landmark between claps, which may prevent long intervals from compressing or stretching. This changes temporal resolution; the prior silent-gap route instead asks learners to sustain the original beat interval without external support.

Use the instructor’s metronome, clapping, and paper with numbered beats and smaller ‘and’ marks. Assume learners can speak the subdivision comfortably at a slow tempo. All eight speak and clap collectively. Keep voices quiet enough to hear clicks; no one performs alone.

Session 1, 30 minutes: five establish a slow beat; five hear the instructor demonstrate evenly and unevenly spaced claps; fifteen alternate clapping every beat with quietly speaking its halfway points; five review what changed. The click marks the numbered beat, not the spoken ‘and.’

Session 2: five review, ten clap paper-marked patterns while speaking every subdivision, ten alternate spoken and silently imagined subdivisions, and five review. Keep expected clap positions explicit. Drift means successive contacts move progressively against clicks. A missing contact with later contacts still aligned is an omission; a written rest is intentional. Restore audible subdivisions for drift. For omissions, retain all spoken positions while simplifying the clap pattern, then restore it.

Session 3: five warm up, ten practise with progressively less audible counting, ten assess unfamiliar patterns, and five reflect. Finish with clapping alone so that simultaneous speech is not a permanent requirement. If speaking creates extra misses, slow down once; if the problem persists, use ordinary beat counting. The method may help interval estimation while burdening attention, and its benefit may disappear when speech stops.
EXPAND.experiment: The instructor compares subdivision with ordinary numbered-beat counting on two matched unfamiliar patterns in session 3. Draw the method assignment, allow three minutes per method, then assess each pattern with clapping alone against clicks. Separately mark drift, omitted expected contacts, and uncertainty. Compare these results with brief first attempts made before either practice treatment. Use private paper marks to check whether counting felt manageable. End subdivision practice if learners cannot hear the click or omissions increase on two consecutive short rounds. If it produces no better transfer than ordinary counting, or improves drift while worsening omissions, the extra speech has no demonstrated overall advantage.

EXPAND.title: Learn short rhythm units before joining the whole pattern
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: reduce sequence-memory demands by learning short units to fluency, then joining them with deliberate practice across their boundaries. Beginners may know the beat yet lose their place while decoding a long pattern. Short-unit learning targets that bottleneck rather than changing pulse reference or teaching error labels.

The instructor prepares paper showing eight numbered positions, divided into two four-beat units. Use only clapping and the owned metronome. Assume each short unit is manageable at a comfortable tempo. All eight rehearse together, and unit boundaries are organizational marks, not extra rests.

Session 1, 30 minutes: five establish the pulse, five hear the complete pattern, ten rehearse each unit, five join them, and five listen for what happens at the join. Include steady instructor demonstrations of both an omitted clap and progressive drift so the group can distinguish them.

Session 2: five review, ten practise the last two beats of one unit flowing into the first two of the next, ten perform complete patterns without stopping at boundaries, and five reflect. If an expected contact disappears but subsequent positions remain aligned, repeat the difficult unit while counting every position. If spacing progressively changes, return briefly to all-beat clapping against clicks before restoring the sequence. Never restart publicly because of one learner’s error.

Session 3: five warm up, ten learn another pattern with fewer grouping marks, ten check unfamiliar patterns, and five reflect. Keep the full numbered strip available even when grouping marks fade. If joins cause pauses, spend the next round on continuous boundary crossing rather than more isolated repetitions. This approach assumes memory or decoding contributes to unevenness; it may offer little when a learner already remembers the sequence but cannot maintain tempo.
EXPAND.experiment: The instructor assigns two matched unfamiliar patterns by paper draw: one receives four minutes of unit-and-join practice, the other four minutes of whole-pattern listen–choose–repair practice. Hear a short initial attempt and a final complete attempt for each against clicks. Tally drift and omissions separately, and mark boundary pauses as an additional cost. Stop isolated-unit practice if pauses persist after two boundary-crossing rounds; return to continuous whole-pattern work. If unit practice does not reduce omissions or worsens continuity compared with the prior route, its memory benefit is unsupported. Pattern differences and group masking limit this small comparison.

EXPAND.title: Practise small timing corrections without a group chase
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: reduce overcorrection. A slightly late clap can provoke a large catch-up adjustment, followed by another adjustment from others, making the group lurch. Learners practise returning toward the metronome through modest changes over several beats instead of inserting an extra clap or sharply compressing the next interval. This targets correction size, a step left unspecified by the prior error-recognition route.

Use the owned metronome, clapping, and eight numbered paper positions. Assume clicks remain audible and the instructor can demonstrate a small timing offset without changing the pattern. Everyone practises together; nobody is identified as the source of an error. Deliberate offsets come only from the instructor.

Session 1, 30 minutes: five establish steady clapping, five hear instructor demonstrations of abrupt versus gradual return, fifteen practise steady four-beat runs after the instructor’s slightly early or late opening clap, and five discuss which returns sounded smoother. Keep offsets small; learners continue following clicks.

Session 2: five review, ten practise gradual realignment on all-beat clapping, ten use sparse marked patterns, and five reflect. Distinguish drift from omission: progressive displacement calls for a small spacing adjustment; an absent expected clap followed by aligned contacts calls for continuing at the next position, without adding a catch-up clap. For large displacement or uncertainty, the instructor gives a collective fresh count-in rather than prolonging a confused attempt.

Session 3: five warm up, ten practise without deliberately introduced offsets, ten check unfamiliar patterns, and five reflect. Feedback concerns the group’s return and spacing. Stop induced-offset practice if learners begin following the instructor’s offset instead of the click. This route is most plausible where correction itself creates unevenness; evidence that this is the group’s main problem is initially incomplete.
EXPAND.experiment: The instructor compares two matched unfamiliar patterns after equal three-minute practice periods: gradual-return coaching for one and the prior classify-and-repair routine for the other, assigned by paper draw. Assess ordinary performances against clicks, with no planted error during assessment. Mark drift, omissions, abrupt catch-up intervals, and whether the group becomes steadily aligned again. Also record how much rehearsal time recovery consumes. Stop the new exercise if two consecutive rounds show more catch-up claps or require a fresh count-in. If smoother recovery takes longer without improving final alignment, or missed events increase, the added correction procedure has not improved the overall result. A single group supports only a practical teaching decision.

EXPAND.title: Give uncertain diagnoses a usable recovery path
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade of “Hear the error, choose the repair.” Preserve private listening choices, instructor demonstrations, collective performance, and separate repairs for drift and omissions. Change the previously unresolved “unclear” response into a bounded rehearsal decision owned by the instructor.

Use the owned metronome and paper showing eight numbered positions and the choices spacing, missing, and unclear. Explain that drift means successive claps move progressively against clicks; an omission means an expected clap disappears while later contacts retain their positions. Written rests are intentional. Never identify a learner publicly.

Session 1: five minutes establish pulse, ten classify instructor examples including correct performances, ten practise matching repairs, and five review. Session 2: five review, ten diagnose fresh examples, ten use the recovery procedure, and five reflect. Session 3: five warm up, ten use listen–choose–retry on familiar patterns, ten check unfamiliar patterns, and five reflect.

The changed procedure is: when group sound is ambiguous or private choices disagree, the instructor withholds an error label and leads one eight-beat round of all-beat clapping against clicks. If this drifts, practise steady spacing before restoring the pattern. If it remains aligned, restore the pattern while counting every numbered position, targeting lost places without claiming that omissions were proven. After two unsuccessful retries, simplify to fewer marked claps at the same tempo; if confusion continues, give a fresh collective count-in and return to the last manageable pattern.

This assumes the instructor can hear group alignment and learners can follow the numbered strip. The added diagnostic round costs rehearsal time but may prevent repeated practice of an inappropriate repair. It cannot identify individual difficulties or fully separate mixed errors.
EXPAND.experiment:
The instructor records a brief baseline in session 1 and a final check in session 3 using different, previously unused eight-beat patterns matched for clap count and rests. Give the same count-in, explanation, and metronome support. On paper, tally clearly empty expected positions separately from progressive displacement; mark ambiguous attempts as uncertain. Include private classification of fresh instructor examples to check hearing as well as performance.

First trial the new branch during session 2 on at most three ambiguous rounds. Record whether the next full-pattern attempt becomes more aligned or has fewer missing events, and how many retries it consumes. Stop the branch after two failed retries and use the stated simplification. Compare its practical usefulness with the source’s ordinary classify-and-repair cycle; improvement on new patterns is encouraging, but one group cannot establish that this added branch caused it.

EXPAND.title: Check that the shared pulse is actually audible
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade of “Build rhythm around a shared pulse role.” Preserve two groups of four, frequent role rotation, metronome-supported practice, unsupported rounds followed by a reference check, and final full-group transfer. The changed action checks the source’s essential assumption that the pulse and pattern layers remain distinguishable before using the pulse subgroup as feedback.

The instructor owns this check. Use only clapping, the existing metronome, and an eight-position paper strip. Assign roles by seating, never ability. At the beginning of each session, hear four beats from the pulse group alone, four from the pattern group alone, then eight together. Everyone privately marks whether they could still hear the pulse layer and the click. If either is lost, lower pattern-clap volume and retry once. If it remains unclear to learners or instructor, abandon divided roles for that session and use whole-group clapping against audible clicks. Do not diagnose errors against an inaudible reference.

Session 1: five minutes establish pulse, five demonstrate drift versus omission, three check audibility, twelve rotate roles, and five review. Session 2: five review and repeat the brief check, twenty alternate supported and short unsupported rounds with role swaps, and five reflect. Restore clicks after unsupported rounds; if the pulse group drifted, reset everyone together. For omissions, retain all eight positions while simplifying marked events. Session 3: five warm up and check, ten rotate roles, five perform together, and ten assess unfamiliar patterns with everyone on the same part.

This retains the mechanism of reducing simultaneous demands. Compared with the source, it spends a few minutes checking whether its reference can function and provides an immediate fallback. It assumes beginners can report basic audibility; hearing two layers still does not guarantee accurate comparison, and quieter playing may reduce engagement.
EXPAND.experiment:
In session 1, bound the audibility trial to the initial check and one volume adjustment. If the pulse or clicks remain obscured, stop divided-role practice immediately and use the fallback. Note how much rehearsal time the check consumes.

For the session 3 transfer check, reserve two matched unfamiliar patterns. Give each a brief first attempt with everyone together. Assign one three minutes of divided-role practice and the other three minutes of whole-group click practice by paper draw, provided the audibility check passes. Assess both with everyone together under identical click support. Tally omissions, progressive displacement, and uncertain cases separately. If divided roles help only while the reference subgroup remains present, transfer is unsupported. If checking and adjusting audibility repeatedly consumes more than three minutes, use the simpler whole-group method for the remaining sessions.

EXPAND.title: Make the reference audible by reducing clap masking
EXPAND.proposal:
New mechanism: improve the sound information available during performance. Loud collective claps can cover the metronome and nearby timing differences. Brief, quiet fingertip-to-palm claps may let beginners hear their relationship to the reference while still producing the rhythm. This changes acoustic masking rather than adding counting, movement preparation, subgroup roles, or an error-classification curriculum.

Use one instructor, all eight beginners, the owned metronome, and numbered paper patterns. Assume quiet clapping is comfortable and the room permits the click to be heard. All work remains collective; private paper marks report whether clicks were audible. Nobody is asked to demonstrate alone.

Session 1: five minutes establish a comfortable pulse, five hear instructor examples of progressive drift and a missing expected clap, ten alternate ordinary-volume and quiet clapping on the same simple pattern, five practise corrections, and five review. Keep tempo and pattern fixed during volume comparisons. Drift calls for restoring even spacing against clicks; a missed event calls for continuing to the next numbered position without inserting a catch-up clap.

Session 2: five warm up, fifteen alternate quiet listening rounds with ordinary-volume transfer rounds, five practise paper-marked rests, and five reflect. The instructor asks for a private audibility mark after each pair. If quiet claps become difficult to hear or produce, increase them slightly once. If the click still cannot be heard, pause clapping, listen to four clicks, and restart a simpler pattern together.

Session 3: five warm up, ten alternate quiet and ordinary rounds with fewer reminders, ten check unfamiliar patterns, and five reflect. The intended gain is better immediate timing feedback without requiring an additional mental task. Compared with ordinary clapping, the cost is less practice at normal rehearsal volume; quiet-clap success may fail to transfer. This route is useful only if masking is a real obstacle.
EXPAND.experiment:
The instructor first compares two eight-beat rounds at ordinary and quiet volume with the same tempo and pattern. Continue the method only if private marks indicate clearer click audibility and the instructor can still hear expected contacts. Stop after one adjustment if neither condition holds.

Reserve two matched unfamiliar patterns for session 3. Hear an ordinary-volume first attempt of each, then give one three minutes of quiet-clap practice and the other three minutes of ordinary-clap practice, assigned by paper draw. Assess both at ordinary volume with identical metronome support. Separately tally progressive displacement, clearly omitted contacts, and uncertainty. Stop quiet practice if omissions increase on two consecutive rounds or anyone reports discomfort. Clearer audibility without improved ordinary-volume performance supports the acoustic premise but does not demonstrate the desired transfer.
